“Billions already spent, pero hanggang ngayon, baha pa rin—nasaan ang flood master plan?”

In 2012, the Philippine government proudly unveiled the ₱351-billion Flood Management Master Plan for Metro Manila and its surrounding provinces. Backed by the World Bank and JICA, approved by the NEDA Board, and anchored on both engineering and governance reforms, it was designed as a generational blueprint: dams in the Marikina River basin, reinforced dikes, stronger pumping stations, and institutional reforms to make Metro Manila more resilient to floods.

But today, amid relentless flooding and billions already poured into projects, the nation is left asking: Where is that master plan now?

A Plan Without a Handover

Palace officials and DPWH Secretary Manny Bonoan recently admitted they received no turnover of the Aquino-era master plan from former Secretary Mark Villar. No documents, no ceremonial handover, no clear roadmap. In the bureaucratic world of public works, where continuity is crucial, this absence is not a minor detail—it is a gaping hole in accountability.

Former DPWH chief Rogelio Singson insists the plan existed and was lodged within the agency’s records. If so, why was there no formal handoff between outgoing and incoming leadership? Why is the government now scrambling to locate a framework that should have been preserved, protected, and actively implemented?

Billions Spent, Floods Still Here

Between 2022 and 2025, more than ₱500 billion has been spent on flood control projects. Yet Metro Manila still drowns at the first sign of heavy rain. Reports of ghost projects, overpriced contracts, and collapsed flood structures deepen the suspicion that funds have flowed faster than the water ever will. Without the master plan as a guiding map, flood control became a patchwork of projects—vulnerable to politics, corruption, and waste.

The Larger Lesson

This controversy exposes a bigger truth: infrastructure is not just about cement and steel. It’s about institutional memory, transparency, and accountability. Master plans are not personal property; they are public blueprints meant to outlive political terms. When leadership changes, a turnover is not optional—it is essential.

Where Do We Go From Here?

If the master plan truly exists in the archives, it must be produced—now. FOI laws, COA audits, and even donor records can and should surface it. If it cannot be found, then the question becomes darker: was the plan deliberately ignored, misplaced, or erased from institutional memory?

What’s clear is this: floods don’t wait for politics to settle. Metro Manila and nearby provinces remain vulnerable, and every missing page of accountability translates into lives and livelihoods at risk.

House Leaders Seek to Return 2026 Budget to DBM Over “Glaring Errors”

Manila, September 3, 2025 — House Deputy Speaker Ronaldo Puno announced on Wednesday that party leaders have agreed to recommend returning the proposed ₱6.7-trillion 2026 National Expenditure Program (NEP) to the Department of Budget and Management (DBM), citing serious flaws in the spending plan.

“Because we do not know how to deal with it,” Puno told reporters, pointing to what he described as “glaring and illogical” entries in the proposed budget.

According to Puno, the NEP contains redundant allocations, such as funding for projects that were already completed, and inexplicable omissions for multi-year programs that still require financial support.

One cited example was the inclusion of classroom buildings in La Union that had already been finished, while essential flood-control projects in Antipolo and Marikina received either zero allocation or were inexplicably repeated.

Senate Raises Red Flags

The House move comes as senators intensified scrutiny of the budget. Senator Panfilo Lacson flagged ₱51.82 billion worth of “vague, distinct” insertions, which lacked clear location or scope, raising suspicions of possible “ghost projects.”

Meanwhile, Senate Finance Committee Chair Sherwin Gatchalian reported multiple red flags in the DPWH’s ₱875-billion proposed budget, including duplicate line items, incomplete descriptions, and suspiciously uniform cost entries.

Senator Erwin Tulfo warned that these anomalies carried echoes of past pork-barrel controversies.

Malacañang Orders Review

Reacting to mounting concerns, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has ordered a “sweeping review” of the DPWH budget under the 2026 NEP. The Palace said it is committed to ensuring transparency and accountability before the spending plan moves forward in Congress.

Next Steps

House leaders stressed that sending the NEP back to the DBM was the prudent course of action.

“We would rather be criticized for being too strict in our review than be accused of negligence later on,” Puno added.

The DBM is now expected to revise and resubmit the budget, delaying congressional deliberations but potentially preventing what lawmakers warn could become the “most flawed budget proposal in recent history.”

Metro Manila once again faced heavy flooding this Habagat season. In a recent episode, PGMN anchor Orion Perez Dumdum explained that the capital’s flooding problem has been recurring for centuries and was already documented as early as the Spanish colonial period.

Orion cited records from Spanish authorities and Jesuit scientists in the 1800s, which identified several districts in Manila as vulnerable to severe floods. 

Areas such as Sampaloc, Binondo, Santa Cruz, Quiapo, Malate, Ermita, and Arroceros were marked as unsafe for permanent settlement due to recurring inundations. 

Parts of Marikina Valley, along with floodplains in Cainta, Taytay, and Pasig, were also recognized as danger zones and were historically used as rice fields because of their naturally waterlogged conditions.

He noted that these early warnings were later reflected in urban development plans, including Daniel Burnham’s 1905 Manila Plan and the World Bank–funded Metroplan of 1977 led by architect and urban planner Felino Palafox Jr. Despite the proposals, Orion said most long-term flood control measures were not carried out, leaving Metro Manila vulnerable to recurring disasters.

Drawing a comparison with Singapore, Orion pointed out how the city-state once faced similar flooding but invested heavily in prevention. 

The government built deep and wide canals, expanded esteros, and reinforced waterways to divert heavy rainfall toward reservoirs and the sea. 

These investments, he said, reduced the city’s flooding incidents even though Singapore receives more annual rainfall than Metro Manila.

In contrast, Orion explained, flood management in the Philippine capital has been undermined by rapid population growth and unregulated settlements. 

Many waterways have been blocked by informal housing, while some residential subdivisions were built on former rice fields and floodplains, areas historically prone to inundation.

Orion also highlighted governance as a major obstacle. With 17 local government units operating independently in Metro Manila, he said coordination on flood control projects has been slow and often inconsistent.

 The absence of a central metropolitan authority, Orion added, has caused delays and conflicts in the approval of large-scale infrastructure.

“Hindi natin masosolusyunan ang problema ng pagbaha kung hindi natin babaguhin ang ating bulok na sistema,” Orion said, emphasizing that structural reforms are necessary.

He warned that without long-term planning and continuity, projects such as the dredging of Laguna de Bay or the construction of spillways will remain unfinished, leaving Metro Manila exposed to the same cycle of floods year after year.

Here’s a detailed and accessible analysis based on the scientific findings of the UP Resilience Institute under Dr. Mahar Lagmay, integrating meteorological data, urban planning insights, and climate resilience principles. 

🌧️ Scientific Analysis of the August 2025 Quezon City Floods

Based on the findings of Dr. Mahar Lagmay and the UP Resilience Institute

1. 📍 Why Quezon City Was Hit Hardest

The flooding was not Metro Manila-wide—it was hyperlocalized.
Rainfall data from multiple weather stations across the region revealed that:

• Quezon City and Nangka, Marikina received an extraordinary concentration of rainfall, while other areas remained relatively unaffected.

• This anomaly underscores the importance of localized weather monitoring and targeted urban planning.

2. 🌊 Rainfall Intensity and Volume

The numbers were staggering:

Metric Value 
Total Rainfall (24 hours) = 141 mm 
Peak Rainfall Intensity = 121 mm/hour 
Peak Time = 2:00 PM – 3:00 PM 

Comparison: Typhoon Ondoy ~90 mm/hour (still under review) 

This means Quezon City experienced more intense rainfall in one hour than what many cities receive in an entire day. 

The sheer volume overwhelmed even well-designed drainage systems.

3. 🏙️ Why the Streets Flooded So Quickly

The flooding wasn’t just due to rain—it was due to rainfall delivered too fast for the city’s infrastructure to absorb or redirect.

• Urban surfaces like concrete and asphalt are impermeable, preventing natural absorption.

• Drainage systems, even those recently upgraded, were not designed for this level of intensity.

• The short burst of extreme rainfall created flash flood conditions, especially in low-lying and densely built areas.

4. 📐 Was This Foreseen?

Yes—and this is where science meets governance.

• The Drainage Master Plan of Quezon City, developed in partnership with the UP Resilience Institute, had already identified the flood-prone zones that were affected.
• These areas were mapped using flood hazard simulations, historical rainfall data, and urban topography.
• Residents in these zones had been informed and capacitated to respond, but the scale and speed of the rainfall exceeded typical preparedness thresholds.

5. 🔬 Scientific Takeaways

• Localized Climate Events: Urban flooding is increasingly driven by microclimate anomalies—not just typhoons or seasonal monsoons.

• Peak Intensity Matters: Infrastructure must be designed not just for total rainfall, but for peak hourly intensity, which is often the tipping point.

• Drainage Planning Must Be Dynamic: Static plans must evolve with climate data, urban expansion, and real-time monitoring.

🛠️ Recommendations Moving Forward

1. Real-Time Rainfall Monitoring: Expand localized rain gauge networks and integrate with early warning systems.

2. Infrastructure Audit: Ensure all flood control projects align with the Drainage Master Plan and undergo environmental impact assessments.

3. Nature-Based Solutions: Incorporate green infrastructure—bioswales, permeable pavements, and retention parks—to absorb excess water.

4. Community Engagement: Continue capacitating residents in high-risk zones with drills, education, and access to emergency resources.

5. Climate-Adaptive Governance: Treat flooding not as a seasonal nuisance but as a climate resilience challenge requiring inter-agency coordination.

Dr. Lagmay’s analysis is a wake-up call—not just about rainfall, but about readiness. The science was sound. 

The warnings were clear. 

Now, the challenge is to ensure that governance keeps pace with climate reality.

This statement from Sec Vince Dizon is more than just a managerial decision—it’s a political act. Let’s peel it like an onion

The Message Between the Lines

By saying “hindi puwedeng imbestigahan ng ahensya ang sarili nito”, Dizon is openly admitting what everyone already suspects: the DPWH’s internal investigations are nothing more than foxes guarding the chicken coop. He’s not just dissolving a task force, he’s declaring war on a culture of self-policing that has long served as camouflage for corruption.

Political Optics

This is a smart opening gambit for a newly minted DPWH chief. Dizon is sending a message: “I won’t play the old games.” It distances him from Bonoan’s tenure and signals to Malacañang that he’s serious about reform. But here’s the catch—bold statements are easy; institutional change is a monster. Will he go beyond slogans and actually call in the Ombudsman, COA, or even independent watchdogs to probe the billions in “ghost” flood projects? Or is this just rhetoric to buy political credit?

Historical Parallels

We’ve seen this movie before. From Marcos Sr. to Arroyo to Duterte, secretaries often promise “house cleaning,” but the broom always misses the dust under the rug. Llamas would probably quip: “Ang DPWH ay parang Pasig River—laging nililinis sa press release, pero pag-ulan, balik sa dating gawi.” The real question is whether Dizon is willing to break the cycle or just repeat the choreography.

The Political Economy Angle

This isn’t just about bureaucracy—it’s about money. DPWH is the motherlode of pork, insertions, and “ghost” projects. By dismantling the internal unit, Dizon could be opening the door to external scrutiny, which might rattle lawmakers who treat flood control as their personal ATM. In other words, he’s poking the hornet’s nest of congressional pork politics. Brave, yes—but also risky.

Vince Dizon just drew a line in the sand. The problem is, in Philippine politics, that line often gets washed away by the next flood—sometimes literal, more often political.

COA FLAGGED QUESTIONABLE FLOOD CONTROL PROJECTS AS EARLY AS 2016

The Commission on Audit (COA) had already identified questionable flood control projects as early as 2016, but many of its findings were left unaddressed, allowing irregularities to persist until they erupted into the multi-billion-peso scandal now under investigation by the House of Representatives.

House Deputy Majority Leader and Manila 1st District Rep. Ernix Dionisio Jr. pressed COA Auditor Tracy Sunico during Tuesday's hearing, asking if today's ghost projects could be traced back to earlier anomalies.

Sunico confirmed that COA had raised red flags years ago, citing issues such as contractors failing to declare ongoing projects, the same personnel and equipment being assigned to multiple simultaneous contracts, and discrepancies between reported and actual completion.

She noted that in the Department of Public Works and Highways' (DPWH) Project and Contract Management Application, projects often appeared "100% completed" even when on-site validation revealed unfinished or defective work.

Sunico said COA had issued notices of charges, suspensions, and disallowances since 2015-2016 amounting to ₱120 billion. She added that records could go as far back as 2000.

Dionisio said the admission underscored the gravity of the problem. "Mr. Chair, mukhang mas malalim pa 'yun na hukay natin on Day One pa lang. COA seems to be doing their job, pero mukhang napupunta lang sa wala yung mga findings nila until President Bongbong Marcos has rung the bell and raised the alarm sa ating pamahalaan na maraming anomalous na nangyayari," he remarked.

Sunico agreed to furnish the committee with COA's full reports, saying, "Your Honor, makapal po pa siya. Ipiprint po namin at ibibigay po namin kayo."

Manila 3rd District Rep. Joel Chua said Tuesday that the flood control scam now under congressional scrutiny did not emerge overnight but stemmed from questionable budget insertions during the Duterte administration.

Chua, chair of the House Committee on Good Government and Public Accountability and co-chair of the Infra-Comm, warned that unchecked practices paved the way for ghost projects and substandard infrastructure nationwide.

"Sunod-sunod ang mga ulat ng Commission on Audit (COA) mula 2017 hanggang 2020 na naglantad ng ilang libong proyektong delayed, depektibo, o tuluyang hindi naipatupad―na nagkakahalaga ng daan-daang bilyong piso," Chua said at the joint hearing. "Hindi bago ang problemang ito. Ito ay problemang namana, naipon at napabayaan―at ngayon, lumulutang na parang sugat na matagal nang hindi ginagamot," Chua stressed.

"Nandito tayo upang tukuyin kung saan nakakalusot ang katiwalian, paano ito nagiging posible, at sino ang nakikinabang," he said.

“Noong 2018, iniulat ng Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism (PCIJ) ang pagkakasangkot ng ilang malalaking contractor sa mga flood control projects na na-delay o hindi natapos,” he noted.

The Infra-Comm, composed of the Committees on Public Accounts, on Good Government and Public Accountability, and on Public Works and Highways, formally begins its probe into anomalous flood control projects and other infrastructure programs.

Chua said that the flood control scam is not new and added that even Congress had once confirmed the pattern in 2019.

“Noong 2019 naman, mismong House Committee on Appropriations ang nakatuklas na maraming flood control projects ang prone sa tinatawag na budget insertion – mga proyektong isinisingit sa pondo nang walang malinaw na konsultasyon o batayan. “Nagkaroon din ng katiwalian o malfeasance sa pagtala ng mga ghost projects na hindi kailanman binuo ngunit patuloy na kumakain ng pondo,” he said.

Navotas and the Flood Fight: Where Billions in Projects Are Flowing

Navotas has always been defined by water. Nestled along Manila Bay, the city faces the daily challenge of high tides, heavy rains, and flooding that can disrupt lives in minutes. It’s no surprise then that much of its infrastructure planning for 2023 to 2025 is heavily anchored on flood control. But how heavy is “heavy”? 

Let’s dive into the numbers.

Billions for Flood Control

From 2023 to 2025, Navotas lined up 155 infrastructure projects worth a total of ₱5.97 billion. Out of these, 87 projects - or nearly ₱4.19 billion - are focused purely on flood control￼.

That means almost 70% of the city’s entire infrastructure budget is tied to keeping water at bay. For residents, this can feel like both a relief and a question: relief that flooding is being taken seriously, but also curiosity about what else could be done with such a big slice of the pie.

Among the big-ticket items are:

• Floodgates along the Navotas Coastal Dike costing between ₱240M and ₱340M each

• New pumping stations and rehabilitation of old ones, some reaching ₱299M in funding

• An open canal project pegged at ₱120M

These are not small-scale drainage cleanups - they’re massive projects designed to reshape how Navotas manages water.

The Transparency Puzzle

Here’s where it gets interesting: only 34 of these flood projects (worth about ₱838.97 million) are reflected in the government’s https://t.co/7HETL8KpOn transparency portal ￼.

Does that mean the other projects don’t exist? Not at all. The portal is still catching up, especially for upcoming 2025 projects. But for citizens who want to track where funds are going, the gaps can feel like trying to piece together a puzzle with missing parts.

Who’s Building Navotas?

Another trend that stands out is the small circle of contractors handling most of the work. A few names dominate the project list, including:

• Topnotch Catalyst Builders Inc. / One Frame Construction Inc. - ₱120M

• 721 Builders Corporation - ₱96.75M

• Earthwork Builders, Inc. - ₱87.5M ￼

It’s common in many cities for certain contractors to specialize in flood works, but with such large sums and limited players, residents often wonder about competition, efficiency, and long-term results.

Bigger Picture: Senate Blue Ribbon Probe

Today, the Senate Blue Ribbon Committee is in the spotlight for its investigation into flood control projects nationwide. The inquiry aims to ensure public funds are being spent properly and fairly.

In this context, it is timely to take another look at Navotas. Congressman Toby Tiangco’s district has billions of pesos worth of flood control projects on record, and some patterns flagged by reviewers - like the heavy concentration of funds, unusually high-priced projects, and reliance on a handful of contractors - mirror the very issues being probed at the Senate.

This is not to pass judgment, but to remind both public officials and citizens that Navotas’ case is very much part of the national conversation on transparency and accountability.

Looking Forward

At the end of the day, Navotas’ choices reflect its reality: a city that must constantly defend itself from water. Investing in flood control is not optional - it’s survival.

The challenge now is keeping the public looped in. With billions at stake, people want to know not just that projects exist, but that they’re progressing, that they’re effective, and that the benefits reach their communities.

Flood defenses may hold back the water, but transparency and accountability are what will keep trust afloat.

Who Audits the Auditors? A Systemic Failure in Flood Control Oversight

By Dr. Anthony “Tony” Leachon
Physician, Civic Leader, and Independent Health Reform Advocate

For years, the Philippines has poured billions into flood control projects—yet every monsoon season, the same scenes repeat: submerged homes, stranded families, and lives disrupted by waters that were supposed to be managed. The question is no longer just about engineering. It’s about accountability. 

And at the center of that question stands the Commission on Audit (COA).

COA is constitutionally mandated to safeguard public funds. It is the final checkpoint in a system designed to prevent waste, fraud, and abuse. But when audits arrive years after the damage is done—when ghost projects have already been paid for, and substandard infrastructure has already failed—what is the point?

⚠️ The Problem of Delay

Recent reports confirm that COA has launched a sweeping performance audit of flood control projects under the Flood Risk Management and Resiliency Program (FRMRP), following catastrophic flooding across Metro Manila 

The audit will assess whether billions in public funds were spent efficiently and whether these projects achieved their intended goals. But this review comes after the fact—after the floods, after the contracts, after the public outrage.

This is not an isolated lapse. In 2022, COA flagged the MMDA for completing only 14 out of 47 flood control projects—less than 30% 

In 2023, 22 of 58 projects under Metro Manila’s flood management program were delayed by up to 310 days 

These are not just numbers. They are symptoms of a system that reacts instead of prevents.

🕳️ Structural Weaknesses

COA’s audits are often retrospective. They rely on documentation, not real-time verification. By the time irregularities are discovered, the money is gone, the damage is done, and the contractors have moved on. There is no built-in mechanism for preemptive auditing, no real-time oversight, and no public dashboard to track project status.

Moreover, COA itself is not immune to systemic inertia. It operates within a bureaucratic framework that slows down responsiveness. Its findings, while technically sound, often lack the immediacy needed to prevent abuse. And when the agency tasked with accountability becomes reactive, the entire system collapses into a cycle of delayed justice.

🧩 What Went Wrong—and What Will Go Wrong Again

What went wrong is simple: no one was watching when it mattered most. The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) approved projects without sufficient scrutiny. Contractors operated with impunity. And COA, despite its mandate, arrived too late to stop the bleeding.

What will go wrong again is equally clear: unless COA evolves, unless it embraces real-time auditing, public transparency, and cross-agency collaboration, the same failures will repeat. The floodwaters will rise, the budgets will balloon, and the public will continue to pay for infrastructure that doesn’t protect them.

🛠️ The Way Forward

1. Real-Time Oversight: COA must deploy technical teams during project implementation—not just after completion.

2. Public Dashboards: Citizens should be able to track flood control projects, budgets, and timelines in real time.
3. Independent Verification: Third-party engineers and civil society groups must be empowered to inspect and report.

4. Audit the Auditors: A separate integrity body should periodically review COA’s own performance and responsiveness.

The question “Who audits COA?” is not rhetorical. 

It is a moral imperative. 

Because when the watchdog sleeps, the wolves roam free. And in a country drowning in both water and corruption, we cannot afford silence, delay, or complacency.

Let this be the moment we demand more—not just from contractors or agencies, but from the very institutions meant to protect us.
